mergePolicy: retain_correct_existing_blocks; add_missing_modules; never replace full prose with link cards

modules.title: Start with a chord you can name
modules.goal: Locate three chord tones and distinguish a name from a voicing.
body: C major uses C, E and G. Select C in the chord chart and read the note names before using sound. The octave number tells you which occurrence of a note is shown; it is not a finger number.

Choose “Build formula tones” and select C, E and G anywhere in the displayed range. Then choose “Match this example” and match the exact displayed keys. The first task checks note identities; the second checks the particular register.

modules.title: Change the third, keep the other notes
modules.goal: Compare the same root without changing register at the same time.
body: Compare A–C–E with A–C♯–E. Keep A and E fixed and listen to the change in the middle note. The symbol Am names the first collection; A names the major triad.
Use the comparison controls rather than assuming that a mood word defines either chord. A listener’s impression depends on the musical passage as well as the notes.

modules.title: Three different kinds of numbers
modules.goal: Keep fingers, octaves and chord degrees separate.
body: In C4, the number identifies an octave. In a formula such as 1–3–5, numbers describe intervals from the chord root. In a hand diagram, finger numbers identify fingers.

Changing a voicing does not create a universal new fingering rule. Use the specific verified fingering attached to an example when one is supplied; otherwise read the notes and do not treat a blank fingering field as permission to invent one.

modules.title: Find the actual lowest note
modules.goal: Read a slash bass and distinguish it from the chord root.
body: C–E–G and E–G–C contain the same three note names. When E is the lowest sounding note, C/E describes a first-inversion C triad. Root and bass are different fields.
Use actual low-to-high pitches when both hands are involved. A right-hand shape alone does not determine the inversion of a larger texture containing a lower left-hand note.

modules.title: Add a seventh without changing its name
modules.goal: Distinguish C7, Cmaj7, Cm7, Cm7♭5 and Cdim7.
body: Compare the fourth chord tone and the quality of the underlying triad. Do not treat the bare symbol “7” as another spelling of “maj7”.

Choose a named subtype in the seventh reference. Read its formula, then compare the lowest note in each displayed position. A four-tone seventh chord has root position and three inversions, not four inversions.

modules.title: Separate the formula from what is played
modules.goal: Understand a named omission instead of guessing missing notes.
body: Open C13. The formula view lists C, E, G, B♭, D, F and A. The supplied playing example uses C, E, B♭, D and A; G and F are explicitly omitted.

Try both views. In the playing-example exercise, an approved omission is part of that example. In the full-formula exercise, all reference pitch classes are required. Neither task establishes a universal rule for every performance of C13.

modules.title: Read the changed degree
modules.goal: Keep altered intervals and actual key names distinct.
body: Compare C7(♭9) with C7(♯9). They change the ninth in different directions while retaining the major third and minor seventh. The written ♯9 is D♯, even though its piano key is also called E♭.
A generic “alt” label needs a chosen interpretation. This collection offers explicit combinations instead of pretending that one fixed group of notes is the only altered dominant chord.

modules.title: Connect two chords without losing the common notes
modules.goal: Use an explicit transition, not just read a tip.
body: For a first comparison, play C4–E4–G4, then C4–E4–A4. The note names C and E stay in place; G moves to A. The second voicing is Am/C, not root-position Am.
Listen to the two blocks, then loop them at a pace you can follow. Use the common-tone highlight to check the relationship. Try on the piano without trying to satisfy a website speed target.

modules.title: Hear a seventh-chord progression in context
modules.goal: Connect the jazz reference to an actual sequence.
body: Begin with Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 in C major. Compare it with the named Dm9–G13–Cmaj9 color-tone example. Use the displayed formulas and voicing notes to see exactly what changed.
The jazz section is an introduction using particular examples, not an exhaustive style dictionary. Check any altered or omitted note before assuming it comes directly from the selected key.

modules.title: A root and fifth without a third
modules.goal: Use the original power-chord task, with a real output.
body: In the power-fifth reference, C5 contains C and G. Here “5” is part of a chord symbol; it does not mean the single pitch C5. The optional octave-doubled example plays C3–G3–C4.
Because the third is absent, do not label this pair as major or minor. Compare it with the complete C major and C minor examples to hear the added third.

modules.title: Finish a small practice task
modules.goal: Complete a bounded session and understand the feedback.
body: Pick one task: build chord tones, identify the lowest note, match an example, or connect two named voicings. Use reset and show answer deliberately; the session summary distinguishes answers shown from answers solved.
The browser records only interactions with its own controls. A correct click pattern is not evidence that your hand position, timing or acoustic-piano performance has been assessed.
